source.title: How a Bilingual LM Becomes Bilingual: Tracing Internal Representations with Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Tatsuro Inaba; Go Kamoda; Kentaro Inui; Masaru Isonuma; Yusuke Miyao; Yohei Oseki; Yu Takagi; Benjamin Heinzerling

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports results about sparse-autoencoder features, not individual neurons. Those results describe a related representational construct but do not test the claim versions about neuron polysemanticity.
record.gate_note: The study measures feature activation patterns and semantic coherence in SAE decompositions. It does not measure individual neurons or compare neuron polysemanticity across measurement choices; the findings below are recorded as related feature-level results with versions ["none"]. Its discussion of neurons and superposition in related work cites other studies and is not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The study measures sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features in bilingual LLM-jp models (150M to 3.7B), not individual MLP neurons or vision neurons. Its 'monosemanticity' score (1 minus semantic entropy over token entropy) and its mixed-language proportion apply to SAE features, a related but different construct. It does not compare neurons with features, vary architecture or activation function, or test the causes of neuron polysemanticity. The superposition link appears only in related work citing Elhage et al. The lower-layer capacity explanation concerns SAE features and is an untested interpretation.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. Bilingual LMs first learn languages separately, then form bilingual alignments, mainly in mid layers and more strongly in larger models. Injecting bilingual SAE representations from a fully trained model into a mid-training model (3.7B, layer 14) lowers perplexity and improves COMET more than English- or Japanese-specific features.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses TopK sparse autoencoders to analyze bilingual feature formation and intervene on model representations; it does not reproduce the original neuron measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported patterns vary with training stage, layer, and model size. The analysis defines feature activation using a threshold at 70% of each feature's maximum activation and uses a cosine-similarity threshold of 0.1 for semantic clustering, but does not test sensitivity to those measurement choices.

fits_no_version.finding: In the 3.7B model's 14th layer, SAE features move from mixed and low-monosemanticity early in training, to language-specific and high-monosemanticity mid-training, to bilingual and high-monosemanticity late in training. Upper-layer features span longer multi-token sequences.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE feature semantic coherence and cross-language alignment in bilingual LMs change with training stage and layer.

fits_no_version.finding: Late in training, lower-layer SAE features (especially the initial layers) show low monosemanticity and activate on multiple meanings. The authors attribute this to vocabulary size exceeding SAE width, a capacity argument about SAE features, not neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Polysemantic SAE features concentrate in early layers of LMs, possibly because of a vocabulary versus dictionary-size mismatch.

fits_no_version.finding: The smaller 150M model shows weaker mid-layer bilingual alignment, less growth in upper-layer span length, and persistently low lower-layer monosemanticity compared with the 3.7B model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Bilingual SAE feature alignment and context-span features strengthen with model size.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The authors note that SAE interpretability and reliability are concerns and that reconstruction accuracy is imperfect, so their analysis approximates the models' internal representations. The study covers English and Japanese only. The reported layerwise results are shown in figures without numerical values in the text, and uncertainty estimates are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows were extracted for the 440M, 980M, and 1.8B layerwise plots (Figures 12–17). The text describes their behavior collectively as generally similar to the reported mid-layer trends, while the plotted values are figure-only and not numerically stated. The 3.7B/150M results that the text explicitly characterizes as differing are retained.

untested.parts: No vision models or image-classifier neurons are studied.
No measurement of the share of polysemantic MLP neurons; only SAE features of residual or hidden representations are scored.
Lower-layer SAE feature polysemanticity is attributed, without a test, to a vocabulary of about 100k exceeding SAE width. Neither neuron counts nor sparsity are manipulated.
Initialization, regularization and training noise are not examined as causes when capacity is sufficient.
No variation of activation function, architecture or regularization, and no neuron-level polysemanticity versus performance trade-off. Model size and training stage vary only for SAE feature metrics.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not revisited.
It uses a fixed 70% max-activation threshold and a 0.1 cosine clustering threshold without sensitivity analysis, and applies them to SAE features rather than neurons.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. Their states describe the paper's own SAE-feature trends, not any claim version. The paper's use of the word 'polysemanticity' (Section 4.2) refers to SAE features, so it should not be read as evidence on V2 or V3. The Section 5 intervention results (Table 1, Table 4) concern the study's own method and are rightly not recorded as rows.

versions.untested_parts: No image-classifier neurons or vision models are studied.
The study analyzes SAE features in bilingual language models, not the share of MLP neurons that respond to unrelated tokens or contexts.
It does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more features than there are neurons or by superposition.
It does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity when capacity is sufficient.

The study varies model size, layers, and training stage for bilingual feature alignment, but does not compare neuron polysemanticity across architectures or activation functions, or test whether it can be lowered without substantial performance loss.
It does not revisit canonical polysemantic neurons or establish that such neurons detect one shared feature. Its findings concern SAE features.
It uses a specified activation threshold and semantic-entropy procedure, but does not compare measurement choices to test their effect on neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: 3.7B model
rows.operation_detail: Measured SAE feature language distribution and monosemanticity
rows.value: figure only; text reports a high proportion of mixed-language features and low monosemanticity
rows.note: The authors describe early SAE features as activated by tokens from both languages without consistent semantic patterns.

rows.subject: 3.7B model
rows.operation_detail: Measured SAE feature language distribution and monosemanticity
rows.value: figure only; text reports that mixed-language features sharply decline while monosemanticity increases
rows.note: The authors interpret this as increasingly language-specific features with semantically coherent activations.

rows.subject: 3.7B model
rows.operation_detail: Measured SAE feature language distribution and monosemanticity
rows.value: figure only; text reports a resurgence of mixed-language features while high monosemanticity is maintained
rows.note: Examples described in the text include features activated by English and Japanese tokens with related meanings.

rows.subject: 3.7B model
rows.operation_detail: Measured layer-wise mixed-language feature proportion and monosemanticity
rows.value: figure only; text reports decreasing mixed-language proportion and increasing monosemanticity across all layers
rows.note: The reported trends diverge across layers in later training.

rows.subject: 3.7B model
rows.operation_detail: Measured mixed-language SAE feature proportion and monosemanticity
rows.value: figure only; text reports increased mixed-language proportion and decreased monosemanticity compared with the mid layers
rows.note: The authors describe lower-layer SAE features as tending toward polysemanticity and give examples of activations spanning multiple meanings.

rows.subject: 3.7B model
rows.operation_detail: Measured mixed-language feature proportion, monosemanticity, and span length
rows.measure: Mixed-language feature proportion, monosemanticity, and average span length
rows.value: figure only; text reports lower mixed-language proportion than mid layers, further decline in monosemanticity, and increasing focus on longer spans
rows.note: The authors interpret the lower token-level monosemanticity as arising from features spanning multiple contextually connected tokens, with examples of building-material phrases and Japanese addresses.

rows.subject: 150M model
rows.operation_detail: Measured layer-wise mixed-language feature proportion and monosemanticity
rows.value: figure only; text reports that around the mid layers mixed-language proportion decreases while monosemanticity increases
rows.note: The paper says this mid-layer behavior resembles that of the 3.7B model.

rows.subject: 150M model
rows.operation_detail: Measured mixed-language feature proportion and monosemanticity
rows.value: figure only; text reports a smaller increase in mixed-language proportion than in the larger model and less tendency toward high monosemanticity across languages
rows.note: This is the paper's stated comparison of smaller and larger models' bilingual feature alignment.

rows.subject: 150M model
rows.operation_detail: Measured mixed-language feature proportion and monosemanticity
rows.value: figure only; text reports relatively high mixed-language proportion and low monosemanticity
rows.note: The authors interpret this as weaker semantic acquisition in lower layers of the smaller model.

rows.subject: 150M model
rows.operation_detail: Measured average span length by layer
rows.value: figure only; text reports a smaller increase in span length than in larger models
rows.note: The authors infer that upper layers in smaller models capture context-level meanings less effectively.
